pos: n. (betrayal of a sovereign; rendering Hebrew qesher)
etymology: From Latin tradere, to hand over — the same root as traitor and tradition. Treason is handing over what was entrusted.
biblical_def: Treason is betrayal of a sovereign. Athaliah cries it as she is deposed and the rightful heir crowned: “she rent her clothes, and cried, Treason, Treason” (2Ki 11:14) — a usurper accusing the lawful king's restorers of the crime she had committed. Jehu's men proclaim him and the conspiracy is described in the same vocabulary (2Ki 9:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines treason as the highest crime of a civil nature of which a man can be guilty; disloyalty; treachery; the offense of attempting to overthrow the government of the state to which the offender owes allegiance.
webster_full: TREASON, n. The highest crime of a civil nature of which a man can be guilty.
2. Treason is the offense of attempting to overthrow the government of the state to which the offender owes allegiance, or of betraying the state into the hands of a foreign power.
scriptures: And when she looked, behold, the king stood by a pillar, as the manner was, and the princes and the trumpeters by the king, and all the people of the land rejoiced, and blew with trumpets: and Athaliah rent her clothes, and cried, Treason, Treason.
So Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi conspired against Joram. (Now Joram had kept Ramothgilead, he and all Israel, because of Hazael king of Syria.
And he brought forth the king's son, and put the crown upon him, and gave him the testimony; and they made him king, and anointed him; and they clapped their hands, and said, God save the king.
Now the rest of the acts of Zimri, and his treason that he wrought, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
corruption_summary: The guilty party names the crime first, and Athaliah shouting Treason at a lawful coronation is Scripture's clearest picture of accusation as cover.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Kings 11 is a study in inverted accusation. Athaliah had destroyed the seed royal and seized a throne she had no right to; when Jehoiada produced the hidden heir, put the crown upon him, and gave him the testimony, she tore her clothes and cried Treason, Treason. The one word she chose was the exact name of her own six-year offence. The accusation was loud, immediate, and precisely backwards.

The detail worth keeping is what was given to the boy king along with the crown: they gave him the testimony — a copy of the law. Deuteronomy required that a king write out the law for himself and read in it all the days of his life. A coronation that hands a man authority without handing him the word he is under has produced most of the tyrants in Scripture.
roots_summary: Hebrew qesher (H7195), a conspiracy or treason, from qashar, to bind together — the same root as confederacy.
roots_lines: Hebrew qesher (H7195) — conspiracy, treason; 2 Kings 11:14, 9:14, 1 Kings 16:20.
Hebrew qashar (H7194) — to bind, conspire; 2 Kings 10:9, 15:30.
Hebrew eduth (H5715) — testimony; 2 Kings 11:12, given to the king with the crown.
usage: “She rent her clothes, and cried, Treason, Treason” — the usurper names her own crime.
“They gave him the testimony” — the crown handed over with the law.
“His treason that he wrought” — the chronicler's plain record.

pos: n. (a judicial inquiry; rendering Hebrew darash, Greek anakrino)
etymology: From Latin inquirere, to search into. In the KJV inquisition is simply diligent inquiry, without the later historical associations.
biblical_def: An inquisition is a searching inquiry. The law commands one before any capital verdict: “the judges shall make diligent inquisition: and, behold, if the witness be a false witness… then shall ye do unto him, as he had thought to have done unto his brother” (Deu 19:18–19). The psalmist says of God, “when he maketh inquisition for blood, he remembereth them: he forgetteth not the cry of the humble” (Psa 9:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines inquisition as inquiry; examination; a searching or search; and judicial inquiry, official examination.
webster_full: INQUISITION, n. Inquiry; examination; a searching or search.
2. Judicial inquiry; official examination; inquest.
3. In some Catholic countries, a court or tribunal established for the examination and punishment of heretics.
scriptures: And the judges shall make diligent inquisition: and, behold, if the witness be a false witness, and hath testified falsely against his brother;
Then shall ye do unto him, as he had thought to have done unto his brother: so shalt thou put the evil away from among you.
When he maketh inquisition for blood, he remembereth them: he forgetteth not the cry of the humble.
And when inquisition was made of the matter, it was found out; therefore they were both hanged on a tree: and it was written in the book of the chronicles before the king.
corruption_summary: Accusations circulate and are believed on repetition, and the law required diligent inquisition with a penalty falling on the false witness himself.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 19:18-19 builds a deterrent into the process. The judges shall make diligent inquisition, and if the witness proves false, then shall ye do unto him, as he had thought to have done unto his brother. A man who accused another of a capital crime and was found lying received the sentence he had sought. That single provision made casual accusation extremely expensive, and its absence is why reputations now cost nothing to destroy.

Psalm 9:12 puts the same activity in God's hands and attaches an unexpected promise: when he maketh inquisition for blood, he remembereth them: he forgetteth not the cry of the humble. God's inquiry is not merely forensic; it is remembering. The victims whose cases no court took up are the ones specifically not forgotten.
roots_summary: Hebrew darash (H1875), to seek, inquire diligently; Greek anakrino (G350), to examine judicially.
roots_lines: Hebrew darash (H1875) — to seek, search, inquire; Deuteronomy 19:18, 13:14.
Hebrew baqash (H1245) — to seek; Psalm 9:12, when he maketh inquisition for blood.
Greek anakrino (G350) — to examine, judge; Acts 12:19, 1 Corinthians 4:3.
usage: “The judges shall make diligent inquisition” — verdicts require searching.
“Then shall ye do unto him, as he had thought” — the false witness bears the sentence.
“He forgetteth not the cry of the humble” — God's inquiry includes remembering.

pos: n. pl. (experts in the law of Moses; rendering Greek nomikos)
etymology: From law. The New Testament lawyer is not an advocate in court but a professional interpreter of the Mosaic law — a scribe by another name.
biblical_def: Lawyers are experts in the law of Moses. Christ's woe against them is precise: “Woe unto you, lawyers! for ye have taken away the key of knowledge: ye entered not in yourselves, and them that were entering in ye hindered” (Luk 11:52). He also charges, “ye lade men with burdens grievous to be borne, and ye yourselves touch not the burdens with one of your fingers” (Luk 11:46). One tests Him with the question that draws out the good Samaritan (Luk 10:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lawyer as one versed in the laws, or a practitioner of law; and among the Jews, one skilled in the Mosaic law.
webster_full: LAWYER, n. One versed in the laws, or a practitioner of law; one whose profession is to institute suits in courts of law, and to prosecute or defend the cause of clients.
2. In the New Testament, a Jew skilled in the Mosaic law; a doctor of the law.
scriptures: Woe unto you, lawyers! for ye have taken away the key of knowledge: ye entered not in yourselves, and them that were entering in ye hindered.
And he said, Woe unto you also, ye lawyers! for ye lade men with burdens grievous to be borne, and ye yourselves touch not the burdens with one of your fingers.
And, behold, a certain lawyer stood up, and tempted him, saying, Master, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?
But he, willing to justify himself, said unto Jesus, And who is my neighbour?
corruption_summary: Expertise in Scripture is assumed to benefit whoever holds it, and Christ's charge is that these men held the key and used it to lock the door.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 11:52 is one of the sharpest sentences Christ ever spoke to religious professionals: ye have taken away the key of knowledge: ye entered not in yourselves, and them that were entering in ye hindered. The key existed, they possessed it, and the net effect of their custody was that nobody got in — including them. Scholarship that makes the text less accessible to ordinary people has replicated exactly this, however rigorous it is.

The lawyer in Luke 10 supplies the other pattern. He stood up and tempted Christ with a question he already knew the answer to, then, willing to justify himself, asked, And who is my neighbour? The parable that follows does not answer his question; it changes it. He asked whom he was obliged to love, and Christ ended by asking which man proved neighbour to the one who fell among thieves.
roots_summary: Greek nomikos (G3544), skilled in the law; nomodidaskalos (G3547), a teacher of the law; grammateus (G1122), a scribe.
roots_lines: Greek nomikos (G3544) — lawyer, one learned in the law; Luke 7:30, 10:25, 11:45-52, Titus 3:13.
Greek kleis (G2807) — key; Luke 11:52, the key of knowledge.
Greek nomodidaskalos (G3547) — doctor of the law; Luke 5:17, Acts 5:34.
usage: “Ye have taken away the key of knowledge” — custody that locked the door.
“Ye yourselves touch not the burdens with one of your fingers” — loads laid, never lifted.
“Willing to justify himself” — the motive behind a good question.

pos: v. (plotted together; rendering Hebrew qashar)
etymology: From Latin conspirare, to breathe together. A conspiracy is people agreeing quietly — and Scripture's most famous one was against a coat.
biblical_def: To conspire is to plot together. Joseph's brothers do it on sight: “when they saw him afar off, even before he came near unto them, they conspired against him to slay him” (Gen 37:18). Absalom's conspiracy is described as growing strong (2Sa 15:12), and the servants of Amon conspire and slay him in his own house (2Ki 21:23). Psalm 2 asks why the heathen rage and the people imagine a vain thing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conspire as to agree, as individuals, in a design to commit some crime, usually a capital offense; to plot; to hatch treason.
webster_full: CONSPIRE, v.i. To agree, as individuals, in a design to commit some crime, usually a capital offense; to plot; to hatch treason.
2. To agree; to concur to one end.
3. To tend to one end; to agree in producing an effect.
scriptures: And when they saw him afar off, even before he came near unto them, they conspired against him to slay him.

And Absalom sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's counsellor, from his city, even from Giloh, while he offered sacrifices. And the conspiracy was strong; for the people increased continually with Absalom.
And the servants of Amon conspired against him, and slew the king in his own house.
But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.
corruption_summary: Conspiracy is treated as the ultimate explanation of events, and Genesis puts a real one inside a providence it could not defeat.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis records the conspiracy against Joseph without softening it. They saw him afar off, and before he came near they conspired against him to slay him. It was deliberate, collective, and murderous in intent. Nothing in the narrative excuses it, and Joseph names it plainly at the end: as for you, ye thought evil against me. Scripture does not deny that men plot.

What it denies is that plotting is the deepest layer. Joseph's full sentence is the answer to every conspiratorial account of history: but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive. Two intentions ran through the same act, and only one of them determined the outcome. That is the difference between believing in conspiracies and being governed by fear of them.
roots_summary: Hebrew qashar (H7194), to bind, conspire; nakal (H5230), to act craftily — Genesis 37:18 uses it of the brothers' plotting.
roots_lines: Hebrew qashar (H7194) — to conspire, bind; 2 Samuel 15:31, 2 Kings 21:23, Amos 7:10.
Hebrew nakal (H5230) — to plot, deceive; Genesis 37:18.
Hebrew chashab (H2803) — to devise, think; Genesis 50:20, ye thought evil… God meant it unto good.
usage: “They conspired against him to slay him” — a real plot, plainly recorded.
“The conspiracy was strong” — Absalom's growing party.
“Ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good” — two intentions, one outcome.

pos: v. (to demand payment by force; rendering Hebrew nagas, Greek prasso)
etymology: From Latin exigere, to drive out or demand. To exact is to require what may be legally owed but need not be pressed.
biblical_def: To exact is to demand payment. The law limits it in the sabbatical year: “every creditor that lendeth ought unto his neighbour shall release it; he shall not exact it of his neighbour… because it is called the LORD's release” (Deu 15:2). Nehemiah rebukes nobles exacting usury of their brethren and makes them restore it (Neh 5:7,11). John the Baptist tells publicans, “Exact no more than that which is appointed you” (Luk 3:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines exact as to force or compel to pay or yield; to demand or require authoritatively; to extort by means of authority or without pity or justice.
webster_full: EXACT, v.t. To force or compel to pay or yield; to demand or require authoritatively; to extort by means of authority or without pity or justice.
2. To demand of right.
3. To demand of necessity; to enforce a yielding or compliance.
scriptures: And this is the manner of the release: Every creditor that lendeth ought unto his neighbour shall release it; he shall not exact it of his neighbour, or of his brother; because it is called the LORD'S release.

Restore, I pray you, to them, even this day, their lands, their vineyards, their oliveyards, and their houses, also the hundredth part of the money, and of the corn, the wine, and the oil, that ye exact of them.
And he said unto them, Exact no more than that which is appointed you.
But the same servant went out, and found one of his fellowservants, which owed him an hundred pence: and he laid hands on him, and took him by the throat, saying, Pay me that thou owest.
corruption_summary: A legal right to collect is treated as an obligation to collect, and Scripture repeatedly asks creditors to decline a payment they could lawfully compel.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 15:2 does not cancel debts because they were unjust; it releases debts that were legitimately owed, on the seventh year, because it is called the LORD's release. The lender is asked to forgo something he could rightly exact. That is a category most modern ethics has no room for — a lawful claim voluntarily unpressed — and it is the exact shape of the mercy in Christ's parable of the unforgiving servant.

Nehemiah 5 shows the reform in practice and how costly it was. The nobles had been taking usury of their own brethren during a famine; Nehemiah confronted them publicly, made them swear to restore the lands, vineyards, oliveyards and houses, and shook his lap as a sign against any who broke the promise. He also records that he himself required not the bread of the governor, because of the fear of God.
roots_summary: Hebrew nagas (H5065), to press, exact — the taskmasters' verb; nashah (H5378), to lend on interest; Greek prasso (G4238), to exact or collect.
roots_lines: Hebrew nagas (H5065) — to exact, drive, oppress; Deuteronomy 15:2-3, Isaiah 58:3.
Hebrew nashah (H5378) — to lend, exact usury; Nehemiah 5:7, 10-11.
Greek prasso (G4238) — to exact, collect; Luke 3:13, 19:23.
usage: “He shall not exact it of his neighbour” — a lawful claim voluntarily unpressed.
“Restore, I pray you, to them” — Nehemiah's public reform.
“Exact no more than that which is appointed you” — John to the tax collectors.

pos: v. (to advance in rank; rendering Hebrew gadal, Aramaic tsalach)
etymology: From Latin promovere, to move forward. Scripture's promotions are pointedly attributed to God rather than to merit or patronage.
biblical_def: To promote is to raise in rank. The psalmist states the doctrine: “promotion cometh neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south. But God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another” (Psa 75:6–7). Balak offers Balaam promotion to very great honour, and Balaam takes the fee-shaped bait (Num 22:17). Haman is promoted above all the princes, and hanged (Est 3:1; 7:10). Daniel is promoted in Babylon (Dan 3:30).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines promote as to forward; to advance; to contribute to the growth, enlargement or excellence of any thing; and to exalt, to elevate, to raise.
webster_full: PROMOTE, v.t. To forward; to advance; to contribute to the growth, enlargement or excellence of any thing valuable.
2. To excite.
3. To exalt; to elevate; to raise; to prefer in rank or honor.
scriptures: For promotion cometh neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south.
But God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another.
For I will promote thee unto very great honour, and I will do whatsoever thou sayest unto me: come therefore, I pray thee, curse me this people.
After these things did king Ahasuerus promote Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, and advanced him, and set his seat above all the princes that were with him.
corruption_summary: Advancement is pursued as the reward of competence, and Psalm 75 removes every compass point from the equation before naming the one who decides.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 75:6-7 works by elimination. Promotion cometh neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south — and the missing direction is north, which in Hebrew idiom is the direction of God's throne. Every human quarter is ruled out before the answer is given: but God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another. Advancement is not a market outcome; it is a verdict.

Haman's arc is the doctrine in narrative. He was promoted above all the princes that were with him by a king's whim, and he was hanged on his own gallows within a few chapters. Balaam's is the warning about wanting it: promotion to very great honour was the offer, and it bent a prophet who could not curse what God had blessed but kept going back to ask again.
roots_summary: Hebrew gadal (H1431), to make great; rum (H7311), to lift up; Aramaic tsalach (H6744), to prosper — Daniel's promotion in Babylon.
roots_lines: Hebrew gadal (H1431) — to make great, promote; Esther 3:1, 5:11.
Hebrew rum (H7311) — to exalt, lift up; Psalm 75:7, he putteth down one, and setteth up another.
Aramaic tsalach (H6744) — to prosper, promote; Daniel 3:30, 6:28.
usage: “Promotion cometh neither from the east, nor from the west” — every human quarter ruled out.
“He putteth down one, and setteth up another” — the verdict is God's.
“I will promote thee unto very great honour” — the offer that bent Balaam.

pos: n. pl. (those who construct; rendering Hebrew banah, Greek oikodomeo)
etymology: From build, Old English byldan. Scripture's builders are judged by what they reject as much as by what they raise.
biblical_def: Builders construct. The psalm quoted more often than any other in the New Testament concerns them: “The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner” (Psa 118:22), applied by Christ to Himself (Mat 21:42) and by Peter to the Sanhedrin's own faces (Act 4:11). Paul calls himself “a wise masterbuilder” who laid a foundation, warning every man to take heed how he buildeth thereon (1Co 3:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines builder as one who builds; one whose occupation is to build; an architect, a shipwright, a mason, etc.
webster_full: BUILDER, n. One who builds; one whose occupation is to build; an architect, a ship-wright, a mason, etc.
2. A creator.
scriptures: The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner.

Jesus saith unto them, Did ye never read in the scriptures, The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner: this is the Lord's doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes?
This is the stone which was set at nought of you builders, which is become the head of the corner.
According to the grace of God which is given unto me, as a wise masterbuilder, I have laid the foundation, and another buildeth thereon. But let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon.
corruption_summary: Expertise is trusted to recognize what matters, and the men whose profession was building rejected the one stone the whole structure needed.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 118:22 turns on the builders' competence, not their ignorance. These were the professionals; assessing stones was their trade, and they examined this one and set it aside. The rejection was an expert judgment, and it was wrong. Peter says it to the very council that had condemned Christ: this is the stone which was set at nought of you builders, which is become the head of the corner — naming them as the tradesmen who mis-graded the cornerstone.

1 Corinthians 3:10 gives every Christian worker the corresponding warning. According to the grace of God which is given unto me, as a wise masterbuilder, I have laid the foundation, and another buildeth thereon. But let every man take heed how he buildeth. The foundation is settled and unrepeatable; what is at issue is the material added to it, and the fire will make that plain.
roots_summary: Hebrew banah (H1129), to build; pinnah (H6438), a corner — the head stone of the corner; Greek architekton (G753), masterbuilder.
roots_lines: Hebrew banah (H1129) — to build; Psalm 118:22, 127:1, except the LORD build the house.
Greek architekton (G753) — masterbuilder; only 1 Corinthians 3:10.
Greek akrogoniaios (G204) — chief corner stone; Ephesians 2:20, 1 Peter 2:6.
usage: “The stone which the builders refused” — an expert judgment, and wrong.
“Set at nought of you builders” — Peter names the tradesmen.
“Let every man take heed how he buildeth” — the foundation is settled; the material is not.

pos: n. (a metalworker; rendering Hebrew charash)
etymology: Old English smith, a worker in metal. Scripture notes the smith chiefly by his absence — a nation without one cannot arm itself.
biblical_def: A smith works metal. Israel's subjection is measured by their lack: “Now there was no smith found throughout all the land of Israel: for the Philistines said, Lest the Hebrews make them swords or spears” (1Sa 13:19), so Israel went down to the Philistines to sharpen every share and axe. Isaiah mocks the idol-maker: “The smith with the tongs both worketh in the coals… and worketh it with the strength of his arms: yea, he is hungry, and his strength faileth” (Isa 44:12). God says, “I have created the smith that bloweth the coals” (Isa 54:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines smith as literally, the striker, the beater; hence, one who works in metals; and one who makes or effects any thing.
webster_full: SMITH, n. Literally, the striker, the beater; hence, one who works in metals; as an iron-smith; gold-smith; silver-smith, etc.
2. He that makes or effects any thing.
scriptures: Now there was no smith found throughout all the land of Israel: for the Philistines said, Lest the Hebrews make them swords or spears:

The smith with the tongs both worketh in the coals, and fashioneth it with hammers, and worketh it with the strength of his arms: yea, he is hungry, and his strength faileth: he drinketh no water, and is faint.
Behold, I have created the smith that bloweth the coals in the fire, and that bringeth forth an instrument for his work; and I have created the waster to destroy.
But all the Israelites went down to the Philistines, to sharpen every man his share, and his coulter, and his axe, and his mattock.
corruption_summary: Dependence on an adversary for basic tools is the shape of every compromise, and Israel walked down to Philistine forges to sharpen the ploughs they farmed with.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Samuel 13:19-21 is a picture of subjugation more effective than any occupying army. No smith in all Israel, by Philistine policy, so that every Israelite went down to his enemy to sharpen his share, his coulter, his axe, and his mattock — and paid a fee for it. Disarmament by supply chain. The chapter ends by noting that in the whole army only Saul and Jonathan had a sword, and the next chapter has Jonathan attacking a garrison anyway.

Isaiah 54:16 is the answer to fear of any forge: Behold, I have created the smith that bloweth the coals in the fire, and that bringeth forth an instrument for his work; and I have created the waster to destroy. The weapon-maker himself is a creature. That is the ground of the promise that follows — no weapon that is formed against thee shall prosper — and it is a stronger comfort than superior armament would be.
roots_summary: Hebrew charash (H2796), a craftsman in wood, stone, or metal; charash barzel, a smith of iron.
roots_lines: Hebrew charash (H2796) — craftsman, smith; 1 Samuel 13:19, Isaiah 44:12, 54:16.
Hebrew masmer and pim — the fee and the tools of 1 Samuel 13:21.
Hebrew keli (H3627) — instrument, vessel; Isaiah 54:16, bringeth forth an instrument for his work.
usage: “There was no smith found throughout all the land of Israel” — disarmament by supply chain.
“The smith with the tongs… he is hungry, and his strength faileth” — the idol-maker tiring.
“I have created the smith that bloweth the coals” — the weapon-maker is a creature.

pos: n. (service, official ministry; rendering Greek diakonia)
etymology: From Latin ministrare, to serve. Ministration is service rendered in an office — the same Greek word behind deacon.
biblical_def: Ministration is official service. Acts 6 records the complaint that the Grecian “widows were neglected in the daily ministration” and the apostles' resolve to give themselves “continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word” (Act 6:1,4). Paul contrasts two: “if the ministration of death, written and engraven in stones, was glorious… how shall not the ministration of the spirit be rather glorious?” (2Co 3:7–8). Zacharias completes the days of his ministration in the temple (Luk 1:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ministration as the act of performing service as a subordinate agent; agency; intervention for aid or service; and office of a minister, service, ecclesiastical function.
webster_full: MINISTRATION, n. The act of performing service as a subordinate agent; agency; intervention for aid or service.
2. Office of a minister; service; ecclesiastical function.
scriptures: And in those days, when the number of the disciples was multiplied, there arose a murmuring of the Grecians against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily ministration.
But we will give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word.

But if the ministration of death, written and engraven in stones, was glorious, so that the children of Israel could not stedfastly behold the face of Moses for the glory of his countenance; which glory was to be done away:
How shall not the ministration of the spirit be rather glorious?
corruption_summary: Practical service and word ministry are set against each other, and Acts 6 refuses the choice by appointing men so that both could be done properly.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 6 is often read as the apostles declining menial work, which misses what actually happened. A real injustice was raised — widows of one language group were being neglected in the daily distribution — and the apostles neither dismissed it nor absorbed it. They had the congregation choose seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, and appointed them over this business. The practical ministry was not downgraded; it was staffed with the most spiritual men available.

2 Corinthians 3 uses the word for something else entirely: a ministration of death engraven in stones, and a ministration of the spirit. Both are called glorious. Paul does not disparage the law to exalt the gospel; he says the lesser glory had no glory by reason of the glory that excelleth. The comparison is between bright and brighter, which is a far higher view of the law than most who quote the passage hold.
roots_summary: Greek diakonia (G1248), service, ministry — the root of deacon; leitourgia (G3009), public or priestly service, in Luke 1:23.
roots_lines: Greek diakonia (G1248) — ministration, service; Acts 6:1, 4, 2 Corinthians 3:7-9, 9:13.
Greek leitourgia (G3009) — priestly service; Luke 1:23, Hebrews 8:6, 9:21.
Greek diakonos (G1249) — deacon, servant; the office arising from Acts 6.
usage: “Neglected in the daily ministration” — a real injustice, properly staffed.
“Men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost” — the calibre assigned to food distribution.
“The ministration of the spirit… rather glorious” — bright and brighter.

pos: n. (one who shares in a work; rendering Greek koinonos and metochos)
etymology: From part. A partner shares both the labour and the take — and the Gospels use the word of a fishing business that became something else.
biblical_def: A partner shares in a work. James and John are named as “partners with Simon” in the fishing trade, and their boats sink together under the catch (Luk 5:7,10). Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus with a striking phrase: “If thou count me therefore a partner, receive him as myself” (Phm 17), and warns against being partakers with idolaters at their table (1Co 10:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines partner as one who partakes or shares with another; a sharer; and an associate in business, one who has a joint interest.
webster_full: PARTNER, n. One who partakes or shares with another; a partaker; an associate.
2. An associate in any business or occupation; a joint owner of stock or capital.
3. One who dances with another.
scriptures: And so was also James, and John, the sons of Zebedee, which were partners with Simon. And Jesus said unto Simon, Fear not; from henceforth thou shalt catch men.
If thou count me therefore a partner, receive him as myself.
And they beckoned unto their partners, which were in the other ship, that they should come and help them. And they came, and filled both the ships, so that they began to sink.
But I say, that the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils, and not to God: and I would not that ye should have fellowship with devils.
corruption_summary: Partnership in the gospel is described in financial language and rarely in personal ones, and Paul stakes his own standing on a runaway slave being received as himself.
corruption_paragraphs: Philemon 17 is one of the boldest sentences Paul wrote: if thou count me therefore a partner, receive him as myself. Onesimus had run away and was legally at his master's mercy; Paul does not argue slavery in the abstract but interposes his own account — if he hath wronged thee, or oweth thee ought, put that on mine account. Partnership here is not a funding relationship but a willingness to be treated as the offender.

Luke 5 shows partnership becoming something else. James and John were partners with Simon in a business, and after a catch that broke the nets and sank the boats, Christ said, from henceforth thou shalt catch men. They forsook all and followed him. The commercial partnership was real, profitable, and abandoned on the day it succeeded most spectacularly.
roots_summary: Greek koinonos (G2844), a sharer, partner — the root of fellowship; metochos (G3353), a partaker, in Luke 5:7.
roots_lines: Greek koinonos (G2844) — partner, sharer; Luke 5:10, Philemon 17, 1 Corinthians 10:20, 2 Peter 1:4.
Greek metochos (G3353) — partaker, partner; Luke 5:7, Hebrews 3:1, 14.
Greek koinonia (G2842) — fellowship; the abstract of the same root.
usage: “If thou count me therefore a partner, receive him as myself” — standing staked on another man.
“Which were partners with Simon” — a business abandoned at its best moment.
“Put that on mine account” — partnership as assumed liability.

pos: adj. (contemptuous, deriding; rendering Hebrew luts)
etymology: From Old French escarn, mockery. The Hebrew luts gives the scorner of Proverbs — a settled character, not a passing mood.
biblical_def: Scornful describes settled contempt. Psalm 1 places the scornful seat at the end of a progression: “Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful” (Psa 1:1). Proverbs treats the scorner as beyond ordinary correction: “Reprove not a scorner, lest he hate thee” (Pro 9:8), and “a scorner heareth not rebuke” (Pro 13:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines scornful as contemptuous, disdainful, entertaining scorn; and acting in defiance or contempt.
webster_full: SCORNFUL, a. Contemptuous; disdainful; entertaining scorn; insolent.
2. Acting in defiance or contempt; regardless.
3. Treating with scorn or contempt.
scriptures: Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful.
Reprove not a scorner, lest he hate thee: rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee.
A wise son heareth his father's instruction: but a scorner heareth not rebuke.
Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser: teach a just man, and he will increase in learning.
corruption_summary: Mockery is now a rewarded public style, and Proverbs treats the scorner as the one category of person correction cannot reach.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 1:1 describes a drift with three verbs and three postures: walketh in the counsel of the ungodly, standeth in the way of sinners, sitteth in the seat of the scornful. Motion slows to a stop, and the final position is a seat — settled, comfortable, and occupied. Nobody arrives at habitual contempt in a single step; it is the terminus of a road that began with taking advice from the wrong people.

Proverbs 9:8-9 draws the line that governs pastoral effort: reprove not a scorner, lest he hate thee: rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee. Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser. The test of whether correction should continue is what the last correction produced. That is not a counsel of despair but of stewardship — effort spent on the scorner is effort taken from the teachable.
roots_summary: Hebrew luts (H3887), to scorn, mock; lets (H3887), a scorner — a fixed character type in Proverbs.
roots_lines: Hebrew lets (H3887) — scorner, mocker; Psalm 1:1, Proverbs 9:7-8, 13:1, 21:24.
Hebrew laag (H3932) — to mock, deride; Psalm 2:4, 2 Chronicles 30:10.
Proverbs 21:24 defines him: proud and haughty scorner is his name, who dealeth in proud wrath.
usage: “Nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful” — the terminus of a three-step road.
“Reprove not a scorner, lest he hate thee” — correction spent where it works.
“A scorner heareth not rebuke” — the category defined by what it cannot receive.

pos: v. (dealt out in portions; rendering Greek diadidomi and merizo)
etymology: From Latin distribuere, to divide among. Distribution in Scripture concerns both bread and gifts, and the same principle governs both.
biblical_def: To distribute is to deal out. John records that Christ “distributed to the disciples, and the disciples to them that were set down” at the feeding of the five thousand (Joh 6:11) — the multiplication happened in the distributing. Paul says God “hath distributed to every man” his measure (1Co 7:17), and that the Spirit divides “to every man severally as he will” (1Co 12:11). Timothy is charged that the rich be “ready to distribute, willing to communicate” (1Ti 6:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines distribute as to divide among two or more; to deal out; to apportion; to bestow in parts.
webster_full: DISTRIBUTE, v.t. To divide among two or more; to deal out; to apportion, as among a number.
2. To dispense; to administer; as, to distribute justice.
3. To divide or separate, as into classes, orders, kinds or species.
scriptures: And Jesus took the loaves; and when he had given thanks, he distributed to the disciples, and the disciples to them that were set down; and likewise of the fishes as much as they would.
That they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate;
But all these worketh that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will.
But as God hath distributed to every man, as the Lord hath called every one, so let him walk. And so ordain I in all churches.
corruption_summary: Resources are counted before they are shared, and the loaves multiplied in the hands that were giving them away.
corruption_paragraphs: John 6:11 places the miracle inside an action: Jesus took the loaves; and when he had given thanks, he distributed to the disciples, and the disciples to them that were set down. Nowhere does the text describe a pile appearing. The bread increased as it passed from hand to hand, which means the disciples experienced sufficiency only while distributing. Andrew's earlier arithmetic — what are they among so many? — was correct and irrelevant.

1 Timothy 6:18 turns it into a standing instruction for the wealthy: that they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate. Paul does not tell rich Christians to stop being rich; he tells them to be permanently poised to hand things over. Ready is a posture word, and it describes a settled disposition rather than an occasional act.
roots_summary: Greek diadidomi (G1239), to distribute or hand round; merizo (G3307), to divide into parts; eumetadotos (G2130), ready to distribute.
roots_lines: Greek diadidomi (G1239) — to distribute; John 6:11, Luke 18:22, Acts 4:35.
Greek merizo (G3307) — to divide, distribute; 1 Corinthians 7:17, Romans 12:3.
Greek eumetadotos (G2130) — ready to distribute; only 1 Timothy 6:18.
usage: “He distributed to the disciples” — the bread grew in the giving.
“Ready to distribute, willing to communicate” — a posture, not an occasion.
“Dividing to every man severally as he will” — the Spirit's own apportioning.

pos: n. pl. (those who perform; rendering Greek poietes)
etymology: From do. The Greek poietes also means a poet — a maker. A doer of the word is one who produces something from it.
biblical_def: Doers perform rather than merely hear. James builds his letter on it: “But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves” (Jas 1:22), and adds the mirror: a hearer only is like a man beholding his natural face in a glass, who goes away and straightway forgets what manner of man he was (Jas 1:23–24). Paul says “not the hearers of the law are just before God, but the doers of the law shall be justified” (Rom 2:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines doer as one who does; one who performs or executes; an actor; an agent.
webster_full: DOER, n. One who does; one who performs or executes; an actor; an agent.
2. One who performs what is required; one who observes, keeps or obeys, in practice.
scriptures: But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
For if any be a hearer of the word, and not a doer, he is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass:
For he beholdeth himself, and goeth his way, and straightway forgetteth what manner of man he was.
corruption_summary: Hearing is mistaken for obeying because it feels like engagement, and James says the deception is specifically self-directed.
corruption_paragraphs: James 1:22 names the mechanism precisely: be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves. The deceit is not practised on anyone else. A person who listens attentively to good preaching, agrees with it, and is moved by it experiences all the sensations of obedience without any of the substance, and the feeling is what does the deceiving. Nobody else is fooled for long.

The mirror image explains why it happens. He beholdeth himself, and goeth his way, and straightway forgetteth what manner of man he was. A mirror shows what needs attention; its whole use is to prompt an action within the next minute. Walking away from the glass unchanged is not a failure of memory but a failure to treat the reflection as actionable. That is why James's blessing goes to the man who continueth — and is a doer of the work.
roots_summary: Greek poietes (G4163), a doer or maker — also the word for poet; akroates (G202), a hearer, an auditor.
roots_lines: Greek poietes (G4163) — doer, performer; James 1:22-25, 4:11, Romans 2:13.
Greek akroates (G202) — hearer; James 1:22-25, Romans 2:13.
Greek paralogizomai (G3884) — to deceive by false reasoning; James 1:22, deceiving your own selves.
usage: “Doers of the word, and not hearers only” — the deceit is self-directed.
“Straightway forgetteth what manner of man he was” — a mirror walked away from.
“The doers of the law shall be justified” — Paul's premise before Romans 3.

pos: v. (openly claiming; rendering Greek epaggello and phasko)
etymology: From Latin profiteri, to declare publicly. A profession is a claim made out loud, which is why Scripture keeps testing it against conduct.
biblical_def: Professing is openly claiming. Paul uses it twice with an edge: “professing themselves to be wise, they became fools” (Rom 1:22), and of women “professing godliness” whose adorning should match the claim (1Ti 2:10). Titus states the test: “They profess that they know God; but in works they deny him, being abominable, and disobedient” (Tit 1:16). Hebrews commands holding fast “the profession of our faith without wavering” (Heb 10:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines profess as to make open declaration of; to avow or acknowledge; to declare in strong terms; and to pretend, to make a show of.
webster_full: PROFESS, v.t. To make open declaration of; to avow or acknowledge.
2. To declare in strong terms.
3. To make a show of any sentiments by loud declaration.
4. To pretend; to make a show of.
scriptures: Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools,
They profess that they know God; but in works they deny him, being abominable, and disobedient, and unto every good work reprobate.
But (which becometh women professing godliness) with good works.
Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;)
corruption_summary: A profession of faith is treated as the finished transaction, and Titus supplies the audit — they profess that they know God, but in works they deny him.
corruption_paragraphs: Titus 1:16 is the most uncomfortable sentence in the pastoral epistles for anyone who counts professions: they profess that they know God; but in works they deny him, being abominable, and disobedient, and unto every good work reprobate. The claim was verbal and sincere-sounding; the denial was behavioural. Paul does not suggest the words were insincere at the moment of speaking — he says the works constitute a denial regardless.

Hebrews 10:23 keeps this from producing anxiety, because the holding fast rests on someone else: let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; for he is faithful that promised. The stability of the profession is grounded in the faithfulness of the Promiser, not in the strength of the professor's grip. Both verses are needed — one to prevent presumption, the other to prevent despair.
roots_summary: Greek epaggello (G1861), to profess or promise; phasko (G5335), to assert; homologia (G3671), confession, profession.
roots_lines: Greek epaggello (G1861) — to profess, promise; 1 Timothy 2:10, 6:21.
Greek phasko (G5335) — to affirm, profess; Romans 1:22, Acts 24:9.
Greek homologia (G3671) — confession, profession; Hebrews 3:1, 4:14, 10:23.
usage: “Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools” — the claim reversed the reality.
“In works they deny him” — conduct as counter-testimony.
“For he is faithful that promised” — why the profession is held, not merely made.

pos: v. (changed in form; rendering Greek metamorphoo)
etymology: From Latin transformare, to change shape. The Greek gives us metamorphosis — a change of the thing itself, not of its appearance.
biblical_def: To be transformed is to be changed in essential form. Paul commands it inwardly: “be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind” (Rom 12:2). The same verb describes Christ on the mount — He was transfigured — and the believer beholding glory: “we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory” (2Co 3:18). Satan's ministers, by contrast, are “transformed as the ministers of righteousness” (2Co 11:15) — a different word, meaning disguised.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines transform as to change the form of; to change the shape or appearance; to metamorphose; and to change the natural disposition of the mind.
webster_full: TRANSFORM, v.t. To change the form of; to change the shape or appearance; to metamorphose.
2. To change one substance into another; to transmute.
3. In theology, to change the natural disposition and temper of man from a state of enmity to God and his law, into a disposition of supreme love and obedience.
scriptures: And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.
But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord.
Therefore it is no great thing if his ministers also be transformed as the ministers of righteousness; whose end shall be according to their works.
I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.
corruption_summary: Change is pursued by pressure on behaviour, and Romans 12 locates it in the renewing of the mind — which is slower and goes deeper.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 12:2 sets two verbs against each other: be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind. Conforming is a pressure from outside that shapes the surface; transforming is a change that works outward from the mind. The stated instrument is renewal of thinking, and the stated result is proving what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God. Discernment is downstream of a renewed mind, not of a stronger will.

2 Corinthians 3:18 gives the method, and it is contemplative rather than strenuous: beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory. The looking does the changing. That is why Scripture, preaching, and the ordinances matter more to sanctification than resolutions do — they are where the glory is seen.
roots_summary: Greek metamorphoo (G3339), to transform, transfigure; metaschematizo (G3345), to change outward appearance — the disguise word of 2 Corinthians 11.
roots_lines: Greek metamorphoo (G3339) — to transform; Romans 12:2, 2 Corinthians 3:18, Matthew 17:2, Mark 9:2.
Greek metaschematizo (G3345) — to change appearance, disguise; 2 Corinthians 11:13-15.
Greek anakainosis (G342) — renewing; Romans 12:2, Titus 3:5.
usage: “Be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind” — change working outward.
“Beholding… are changed into the same image” — the looking does the changing.
“Transformed as the ministers of righteousness” — a different word, meaning disguised.

pos: adj. (making no sound; rendering Hebrew damam, Greek sigao)
etymology: From Latin silere, to be still. Scripture's silences are weighted — God's, the accused's, and heaven's.
biblical_def: Silent means without speech. Hannah's is misread by a priest: she spoke in her heart, only her lips moved, and Eli thought her drunk (1Sa 1:13). Isaiah's Servant is silent under injustice: “he was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth” (Isa 53:7), and Christ fulfils it before Pilate — “he answered him to never a word; insomuch that the governor marvelled greatly” (Mat 27:14). Habakkuk commands, “the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him” (Hab 2:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines silent as not speaking; mute; dumb; habitually taciturn; still; having no sound; and not mentioning, saying nothing.
webster_full: SILENT, a. Not speaking; mute; dumb; habitually taciturn.
2. Having no sound; still; having no noise; as the silent watches of the night.
3. Not operative; wanting efficacy.
4. Not mentioning; not proclaiming.
scriptures: He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth.
And he answered him to never a word; insomuch that the governor marvelled greatly.
But the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him.
Now Hannah, she spake in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard: therefore Eli thought she had been drunken.
corruption_summary: Silence is read as weakness or as having no answer, and the strongest man in the Gospels used it before the one court that could have killed Him.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 27:14 records the effect rather than the reason: he answered him to never a word; insomuch that the governor marvelled greatly. Christ was not without a defence — He had answered questions all through His ministry and would answer the high priest's direct oath. The silence before Pilate was chosen, and it fulfilled a prophecy written seven hundred years before about a lamb dumb before her shearers. Restraint of that kind requires more strength than any speech.

Habakkuk 2:20 gives the congregation its own use of silence: the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him. It stands at the end of a chapter of woes against the proud. Silence here is not emptiness but the appropriate response to a Presence, and a worship service with no room for it has removed the one posture Habakkuk prescribes.
roots_summary: Hebrew damam (H1826), to be silent, still; chashah (H2814), to hold peace; Greek sigao (G4601), to keep silence.
roots_lines: Hebrew damam (H1826) — to be silent, still; Psalm 4:4, Habakkuk 2:20, Leviticus 10:3, Aaron held his peace.
Hebrew alam (H481) — to be dumb, silent; Isaiah 53:7, as a sheep before her shearers is dumb.
Greek siopao (G4623) — to be silent; Matthew 26:63, Mark 14:61.
usage: “He opened not his mouth” — silence chosen, and prophesied.
“The governor marvelled greatly” — the effect on a man used to speeches.
“Let all the earth keep silence before him” — a posture worship needs room for.

pos: adj. (fully persuaded; rendering Greek peitho and tharreo)
etymology: From Latin confidere, to trust fully. Biblical confidence is always confidence in something, and Scripture is careful about the object.
biblical_def: Confident means fully persuaded. Paul's assurance rests on God's work rather than his own: “being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Php 1:6). He is “confident… and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord” (2Co 5:8). Proverbs warns that “confidence in an unfaithful man in time of trouble is like a broken tooth, and a foot out of joint” (Pro 25:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines confident as having full belief; trusting; relying; fully assured; positive; dogmatical; and bold to a vice, having an excess of assurance.
webster_full: CONFIDENT, a. Having full belief; trusting; relying; fully assured.
2. Positive; dogmatical; as a confident talker.
3. Trusting; without suspicion of failure.
4. Bold to a vice; having an excess of assurance.
scriptures: Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ:
We are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord.
Confidence in an unfaithful man in time of trouble is like a broken tooth, and a foot out of joint.
For we are the circumcision, which worship God in the spirit, and rejoice in Christ Jesus, and have no confidence in the flesh.
corruption_summary: Confidence is cultivated as a quality of the self, and Philippians grounds it entirely in what Someone else has begun and will finish.
corruption_paragraphs: Philippians 1:6 places every part of the confidence outside the believer: he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ. He began it, He will finish it, and the deadline is fixed. Paul is not confident in the Philippians; he is confident about them, on the basis of a workman who does not abandon projects. That distinction is the difference between assurance and self-esteem.

Philippians 3:3 states the negative side just as firmly: we are the circumcision, which worship God in the spirit, and rejoice in Christ Jesus, and have no confidence in the flesh. Paul then lists his own considerable credentials and writes them off as loss. Confidence has to be removed from somewhere before it can rest somewhere else, and the removal is usually the painful half.
roots_summary: Greek peitho (G3982), to persuade, be confident; tharreo (G2292), to be of good courage; pepoithesis (G4006), confidence.
roots_lines: Greek peitho (G3982) — to be persuaded, confident; Philippians 1:6, 25, Romans 8:38.
Greek tharreo (G2292) — to be confident, bold; 2 Corinthians 5:6, 8.
Greek parrhesia (G3954) — boldness, confidence; Hebrews 10:35, cast not away therefore your confidence.
usage: “He which hath begun a good work in you will perform it” — every part of it outside the believer.
“No confidence in the flesh” — removed from one place to rest in another.
“Confidence in an unfaithful man… a broken tooth” — misplaced trust hurts at the moment it is needed.

pos: v. (to put to death on a cross; rendering Greek stauroo)
etymology: From Latin crucifigere, to fasten to a cross. The word names the most shameful execution Rome had, reserved for slaves and rebels.
biblical_def: To crucify is to execute on a cross. The crowd's demand is recorded without softening: “they cried out the more, saying, Let him be crucified” (Mat 27:23). Paul applies the verb to the believer twice over: “I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me” (Gal 2:20), and “they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts” (Gal 5:24). Hebrews warns of those who “crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh” (Heb 6:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines crucify as to nail to a cross; to put to death by nailing the hands and feet to a cross or gibbet; and to subdue, to mortify, to destroy the power or ruling influence of.
webster_full: CRUCIFY, v.t. To nail to a cross; to put to death by nailing the hands and feet to a cross or gibbet.
2. In scriptural language, to subdue; to mortify; to destroy the power or ruling influence of.
3. To reject and despise.
4. To vex or torment.
scriptures: And the governor said, Why, what evil hath he done? But they cried out the more, saying, Let him be crucified.

I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me.
And they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts.
If they shall fall away, to renew them again unto repentance; seeing they crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh, and put him to an open shame.
corruption_summary: The cross is worn as an ornament and preached as a symbol, and the verb behind it named a public execution designed to be unbearable to watch.
corruption_paragraphs: Galatians 2:20 is the most quoted verse in the letter and the most easily softened: I am crucified with Christ. The tense is past and the image is not a hardship or a discipline but an execution already carried out. What follows keeps it from morbidity — nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God. A death and a life in one sentence, in that order.

Galatians 5:24 assigns the believer an action rather than a status: they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts. Crucifixion was slow, public, and irreversible, and it is chosen deliberately as the picture of what is done to the flesh's appetites. Nothing about it suggests management or negotiation, which is why the New Testament's language about sin is so much harder than most contemporary discipleship.
roots_summary: Greek stauroo (G4717), to crucify; sustauroo (G4957), to crucify together with; anastauroo (G388), to crucify afresh.
roots_lines: Greek stauroo (G4717) — to crucify; Matthew 27:22-23, Galatians 5:24, 1 Corinthians 1:23.
Greek sustauroo (G4957) — crucified with; Galatians 2:20, Romans 6:6.
Greek anastauroo (G388) — to crucify afresh; only Hebrews 6:6.
usage: “Let him be crucified” — the demand recorded without softening.
“I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live” — a death and a life in one sentence.
“Have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts” — not management, execution.

pos: adj. (full of gladness; rendering Hebrew samach, Greek chairo)
etymology: Joy with the intensive ending. Scripture's joyfulness is repeatedly commanded, which assumes it is not merely a temperament.
biblical_def: Joyful means full of gladness. The psalms command it corporately: “Make a joyful noise unto the LORD, all ye lands” (Psa 100:1). Paul, writing from prison, reports being “exceeding joyful in all our tribulation” (2Co 7:4). Isaiah promises that God will make the outcasts “joyful in my house of prayer” (Isa 56:7), and Ecclesiastes counsels, “live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest all the days of the life of thy vanity” (Ecc 9:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines joyful as full of joy; very glad; exulting; and giving joy or pleasure.
webster_full: JOYFUL, a. Full of joy; very glad; exulting.
2. Giving joy or pleasure; as joyful news; joyful days.
scriptures: A Psalm of praise. Make a joyful noise unto the LORD, all ye lands.
Great is my boldness of speech toward you, great is my glorying of you: I am filled with comfort, I am exceeding joyful in all our tribulation.

Even them will I bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer: their burnt offerings and their sacrifices shall be accepted upon mine altar; for mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people.

Live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest all the days of the life of thy vanity, which he hath given thee under the sun, all the days of thy vanity: for that is thy portion in this life, and in thy labour which thou takest under the sun.
corruption_summary: Joy is waited on as a mood, and Scripture keeps commanding it — which means it is available to obedience and not only to circumstance.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Corinthians 7:4 refuses the assumption that joy waits on relief: I am filled with comfort, I am exceeding joyful in all our tribulation. Not after it, not despite forgetting it — in it. Paul had just described being troubled on every side, without were fightings, within were fears. The joy and the fear occupy the same paragraph, which is more honest than either a religion that denies the fear or a realism that denies the joy.

Isaiah 56:7 attaches joy to a place and a people: even them will I bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer… for mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people. The ones addressed are the foreigner and the eunuch — those who had assumed they were excluded. God does not merely admit them; He undertakes to make them joyful there.
roots_summary: Hebrew samach (H8055), to rejoice, be glad; rua (H7321), to shout, make a joyful noise; Greek chairo (G5463), to rejoice.
roots_lines: Hebrew samach (H8055) — to rejoice; Isaiah 56:7, Ecclesiastes 9:9, Psalm 5:11.
Hebrew rua (H7321) — to shout, raise a war cry or joyful noise; Psalm 100:1, 95:1.
Greek chairo (G5463) — to rejoice; Philippians 4:4, rejoice in the Lord alway.
usage: “Make a joyful noise unto the LORD, all ye lands” — joy commanded corporately.
“Exceeding joyful in all our tribulation” — in it, not after it.
“Make them joyful in my house of prayer” — promised to those who assumed exclusion.

pos: n. (a blow; rendering Hebrew makkah and nega)
etymology: From strike. In Scripture a stroke is a blow struck — by an enemy, by a judge, or by God's own hand in chastening.
biblical_def: A stroke is a blow. Job's friend counsels him about God's dealing: “he maketh sore, and bindeth up: he woundeth, and his hands make whole” (Job 5:18), and Job himself asks that God's stroke be removed (Job 9:34; 13:21). The psalmist prays, “Remove thy stroke away from me: I am consumed by the blow of thine hand” (Psa 39:10). Isaiah says of the Servant, “for the transgression of my people was he stricken” (Isa 53:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stroke as a blow; the striking of one body against another; a sudden attack of disease or affliction; calamity; and the sound of a clock.
webster_full: STROKE, n. A blow; the striking of one body against another.
2. A hostile blow or attack.
3. A sudden attack of disease or affliction; calamity.
4. Fatal attack; as the stroke of death.
scriptures: Remove thy stroke away from me: I am consumed by the blow of thine hand.
For he maketh sore, and bindeth up: he woundeth, and his hands make whole.
Let him take his rod away from me, and let not his fear terrify me:
He was taken from prison and from judgment: and who shall declare his generation? for he was cut off out of the land of the living: for the transgression of my people was he stricken.
corruption_summary: Affliction from God's hand is either denied outright or read as abandonment, and the psalmist prays about it directly as a stroke he asks to have lifted.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 39:10 is a prayer few Christians are taught to pray: remove thy stroke away from me: I am consumed by the blow of thine hand. The psalmist does not doubt the source, does not accuse God of injustice, and does not pretend to be fine. He identifies the hand, states the effect, and asks for it to stop. That combination — theological clarity and unedited request — is what most modern prayer lacks in either direction.

Isaiah 53:8 puts the decisive stroke elsewhere: for the transgression of my people was he stricken. The Servant receives the blow that the guilty had earned, and verse 4 records the crowd's misreading — we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted. They were right that God struck Him and wrong about why. The stroke was real, divine, and substitutionary.
roots_summary: Hebrew makkah (H4347), a blow or wound; nega (H5061), a stroke or plague; shebet (H7626), a rod.
roots_lines: Hebrew nega (H5061) — stroke, plague, mark; Psalm 39:10, Deuteronomy 17:8.
Hebrew makkah (H4347) — blow, wound; Isaiah 53:8 in context, Jeremiah 30:14.
Hebrew nagaph (H5062) — to strike; Isaiah 53:4, we did esteem him stricken.
usage: “Remove thy stroke away from me” — the source named, the request unedited.
“He woundeth, and his hands make whole” — the same hands.
“For the transgression of my people was he stricken” — the decisive blow, borne elsewhere.
